Basal metabolic rate in the Southern tamandua (Tamandua tetradactyla) has been measured under controlled laboratory conditions where individuals maintained a body temperature of 33.6 °C [T = 33.6 °C], reflecting the slightly lower thermoregulatory set point typical of many xenarthrans. Under these conditions, the maximum resting oxygen consumption recorded was 885.5 milliliters per hour [JOi = 885.5 milliliters per hour], a value derived from study animals with a mean body mass of approximately 3500 grams at a temperature of 33.6 °C [T = 33.6 °C]. This metabolic rate is notably modest for a mammal of this size, consistent with the characteristically low energy expenditures observed across the order Pilosa. The reduced metabolic demand is thought to be an adaptive response to the species' primarily myrmecophagous diet, which provides a reliable but not particularly energy-dense nutritional base. Such a low basal metabolic rate permits the Southern tamandua to subsist on a diet of ants and termites without needing to forage continuously, thereby conserving energy during periods of inactivity.

Reproductive output in the Southern tamandua is constrained by its slow life-history pace, with females typically producing a single offspring per litter [N_R_i = single offspring per litter]. The maximum observed frequency of these reproductive events approaches approximately 1.4 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.4 litters per year], though this rate is likely realized only under optimal conditions with abundant food resources and minimal environmental stress. The maximum reproductive rate of 1.4 offspring per year corresponds to an inter-birth interval of roughly nine to ten months, which is relatively prolonged for a mammal of this size and reflects the high maternal investment required for each offspring. In wild populations, the actual rate is often lower due to seasonal fluctuations in prey availability and the energetic costs associated with lactation, which can extend over many months.

The mass of newborn Southern tamanduas has been estimated from data on the closely related Tamandua mexicana, given the logistical challenges of weighing wild neonates. Based on those comparisons, the wet weight at birth is approximately 290 grams [Wwb = approximately 290 grams], a relatively small size for a placental mammal that gives birth to a single precocial offspring. Neonates are born fully furred and with their eyes open, allowing them to cling to the mother's back almost immediately after parturition. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult ranges considerably, with maximum recorded values approaching 5000 grams [Wwi = 5000 grams], although typical adults fall between 1.5 and 8.4 kilograms depending on sex, geographic location, and seasonal nutritional status. This wide range underscores the species' capacity for energy storage during periods of plenty.

Life-history timing in the Southern tamandua is tightly linked to the thermoregulatory environment, with a series of developmental milestones documented under captive conditions at a stable ambient temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C]. Under these conditions, gestation time was recorded at 160 days [tg = 160 days], a duration that falls squarely within the 130 to 190 day range reported in the literature and is consistent with the prolonged gestation typical of myrmecophagid xenarthrans at a temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C]. The time since birth at weaning in this species has been documented at 200 days [tx = 200 days], though field observations suggest that nutritional independence may be delayed to as late as one year in resource-poor environments at a temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C]. The lactation period is therefore substantial, requiring the mother to provision the growing juvenile for over half a year before it can forage independently.

The pace of sexual maturation and eventual senescence in the Southern tamandua reflects its position as a slow-living mammal within the comparative framework of neotropical xenarthrans. Under a stable thermal regime of 32 °C [T = 32 °C], the time since birth at puberty was recorded at 365 days [tp = 365 days], meaning that individuals attain reproductive maturity at approximately one year of age. The maximum lifespan documented for this species under similar captive conditions reaches approximately 19 years [am = approximately 19 years], a remarkably long duration for a mammal of its body size and one that aligns with the general pattern of extended longevity seen in anteat at a temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C]ers and sloths. This extended lifespan, combined with a late age at first reproduction and a low annual reproductive output, positions the Southern tamandua firmly at the slow end of the life-history continuum among placental mammals.
